Often also states that the Loewenneims always seemed to have plenty of ready money, and the code indicates that they must have been spending money freely as we may deduce from the fact that the word for money is Wasche (underwear), for 1000 Kleid (clothing or Clothes) and for 2000 Mantel (overcoat). By an appropriate combination of these three words it would be easy to manufacture a sentence relating to the transmission or expenditure of large sums of money.

There is a codeword too for letter of credit --- another implication travels involving the use of much money, while the use of a code word for Postlagernd (post restante) indicates uncertainty of movements.

There is also a codeword for courier, so that we may presume the Loewenneims conveyed messages secretly into Germany or Austria by means of couriers. A risky job, only undertaken by those extremely devoted to the cause or persons well paid for the dangers they ran.

Furthermore, we note that Walter Loewenheim uses five codewords for police. If he was engaged in genuine underground work in Germany, we would expect --- for the sake of very necessary explicitness --- a special word for Gestapo, but there is none. Likewise we would for similar reasons expect a man who had formerly been "in close touch with the Comintern" but had broken away to need a special codeword for G.P.U., but again there is none. Yet five words for the police! One is inclined to wonder whether the Loewenneims were not exactly personae gratae with the police of other countries.

Undoubtedly, as Mrs. Lambert remarks, there is a danger that the Loewenheim code may have passed into wrong hands, with perhaps injury to British interests as well as disastrous consequences to private individuals. But we must also bear in mind the possibility that the Loewenneims may have been using this code to evade the censorship during their internment. It could easily be applied that way, even if the persons concerned corresponded in English, and our suspicions in that respect must be strengthened by the fact that recently Captain Johnson caught Loewenheim in the act of trying to smuggle a message out of Onchan Internment Camp via the wife of a fellow-internee who was on a visit to her husband --- an offence which in addition to prejudicing his chances of release should call for further investigations of his activities during his internment.

I am still trying to obtain information concerning the Loewenneims; meanwhile, I hope that they will not be released. In my opinion, Walter Loewenheim has been shown to be a person who is likely to be dangerous on grounds of security, no matter what political faith he may profess. Previously, I should have been inclined to waive objections to the release of Ernst Loewenheim, whose health is none too good in internment, and of Karthäuser, but in such a case we do not know whether they would not act on instructions received by letter from Walter Loewenheim. We cannot be certain that we have obtained the whole code!
